Through this, the PACS staff operate a small banking window — deposits, withdrawals, and DBT/benefit payouts — inside the village using handheld and Aadhaar-enabled devices, so that unbanked rural households get banking services at their own cooperative. This is the "banking-window / banking correspondent" model promoted for smart PACS. - Cyber safety: with digitisation come data-security duties. The society must keep backups and protect member data; members must not share passwords, OTPs or PINs, and should report suspected fraud to the society, the associated bank, and the local cyber cell. NABARD and state agencies run training and digital-literacy programmes for PACS secretaries and computer operators, together with financial-literacy camps for members. Section 84(2) deems certain matters to be disputes: a claim by the society for a debt or demand due from a member or his nominee/heirs; a claim by a surety against a principal debtor; and any dispute arising in connection with the election of an officer. The question whether a particular matter is such a dispute is decided by the arbitrator, and that decision is final. The arbitrator is **appointed by the Central Registrar** and, unless the Act says otherwise, the **Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996** applies to the proceedings as if they had been referred under that Act. **Section 85 – Limitation.** For a dispute over recovery of a sum (with interest) due to the society from a member, limitation runs from the date the member dies or ceases to be a member. For disputes based on an act or omission covered by clauses (b), (c) or (d) of Section 84(1) the period is **six years** from the act or omission. Election disputes must be referred within **one month** of the declaration of results. All other disputes are governed by the Limitation Act, 1963 as if the dispute were a suit and the arbitrator a civil court. The arbitrator may admit a late reference on proof of sufficient cause. **Section 85A – Co-operative Ombudsman.** The Central Government appoints one or more Co-operative Ombudsmen with territorial jurisdiction to inquire into complaints made by members of multi-State societies about **deposits, equitable benefits of the society's functioning, or any other issue affecting the individual rights of the member**. The Ombudsman must complete the inquiry and adjudication **within three months**, may issue directions which the society must comply with within one month, and possesses the powers of a civil court (summoning witnesses, examining them on oath, discovery and production of books). If the affected area under a notified crop exceeds 25% of the total insured area in the notified insurance unit, all eligible insured farmers of that unit are deemed to have suffered the loss and are compensated on a percentage-loss basis. - **Post-harvest losses.** Coverage for crops kept in the field in "cut and spread" or small-bundled condition for drying after harvesting, for a maximum of **14 days (two weeks) from the date of harvesting**, against hailstorm, cyclone, cyclonic rains and unseasonal rains. Assessment is on an individual-farm basis through loss assessors and a joint survey with State officials. - **Coverage option.** States/UTs may choose which add-on covers (prevented sowing, localized calamity, mid-season adversity, post-harvest) to implement and may even offer single-peril covers such as hail protection. Not all covers are available in every State/district — the State's own notification governs. - **Exclusions.** Losses from war and kindred perils, nuclear risks, riots and malicious damage, theft, and destruction by domestic/wild animals are excluded, as are other preventable risks; post-harvest cover does not apply to crops already bundled/heaped for threshing. ## 2. Central Registrar (1) The Central Government may appoint a person to be the Central Registrar of Cooperative Societies and may appoint such other persons as it may think fit to assist the Central Registrar. (2) The Central Government may, by notification, direct that any power exercisable by the Central Registrar under this Act (other than the power of registration of a multi state cooperative society) shall, in relation to such society, and such matters as may be specified in the notification, be exercisable also by any other officer of the Central Government or of a State Government as may be authorised by the Central Government subject to such conditions as may be specified therein: Provided that no officer of a state government shall be empowered 11 to exercise such power in relation to a national cooperative society. 5. Multi-state cooperative societies which may be registered (1) No multi-state cooperative society shall be registered under this Act, unless, (a) its main objects are to serve the interests of members in more than one state; and (b) its bye-laws provide for social and economic betterment of its members through self-help and mutual aid in accordance with the cooperative principles. Disputes touching the constitution or business of a multi-State society, other than those before authorities under the Act, can be referred to arbitration before the Central Registrar (section 84); his decisions and orders are executed like civil-court decrees (section 94). State societies use their State Acts' arbitration and recovery mechanisms. Governance timeline. Both systems impose five-year board terms, one-member-one-vote, timely elections and annual audit, but for multi-State societies these are reinforced by the central scheme — the Co-operative Election Authority (section 45), the five-year term and the six-month audit window — while State societies follow their State Act, which post-2021 need not replicate Part IXB and varies. Conversion. A State society may convert into a multi-State society by amending its bye-laws to extend its jurisdiction, registered by the Central Registrar after consulting the State Registrars (section 22). On registration it becomes a multi-State society from that date, and the State Registrar must order that it has ceased to be a society under State law. The converse — a multi-State society confining itself to one State — requires it to wind up or reorganise into a State society. Practical consequence. For legal assistance, the answer to any question about a society's membership, elections, board, audit, disputes or winding up turns first on which law registered it: State law and the State Registrar before the courts of that State, or the MSCS Act 2002 and the Central Registrar under Union jurisdiction. ose of clustering is to divide the States into different groups of districts, so that expected sum insured (ESI) becomes low and risk is shared and diversified. State s may form the clusters of districts based on www.pmfby.gov.in Revised Operational Guidelines of PMFBY 63 mixed agro -climatic zones. i) Districts of h igh risk and low risk areas, ii) districts of different agro - climatic zones, and iii) ESI is of each cluster should be of similar order. Prior to the bid invitation, details on the clusters formation may also be made available to the Insurance Companies. The object of Clustering/ Clubbing of districts should be done to achieve the following objectives: • Cluster formation may be applicable for upto 3 years. • Different Clusters may be defined based on risk profile of the district so as to increase the diver sification of risk within a clu ster and enable risk spreading for insurer. • Cluster may contain districts with mixed agro -climatic zones so as to increase the diversification of risk within a cluster. • Crop wise associated risk may also be diversified among the clusters and shall be factored in cluster formation. 1. Hence, one of the major requirements of clustering is risk analysis of different districts. As per 2016 Guidelines of PMFBY, for the purpose of clustering/clubbing of districts and determination of L1 bidder, the risk is analyzed based on long term data of yield by (a) computing average burn cost (percent difference between actual yield and threshold yield) and b) computing the level of variability in long term yield. Since, availability of high quality long term yield data is difficult, especially at lower administrative level, other methods (including use of satellite data) can be tried for risk assessment. 2. Satellite data, of moderate resolution (e.g. Resourcesat AWiFS, Terra/Aqua MODIS) are available, for long term, i.e. at least around 15 years. The long term Vegetation Indices, which are indicators of crop health, derived from these satellites can be used to assess the year to year variations and thereby understanding the risk potential of an area. It can be combined with many other satellite derived products, such as flood maps, drought assessments and vulnerability and long term weather data to carry out the risk analysis. States are advised to take the support of concerned national or State level research organizations (e.g. ISRO - NRSC/SAC, MNCFC, SRSC, SAUs, etc.), to use the above mentioned technology for carrying out risk analysis of the Districts/ Talukas/ Blocks towards improvement in clustering. 3. Most farmers and rural workers have no employer pension, so the government has created very low-cost pension schemes that are collectible through savings accounts and are especially suited to cooperative and rural members. Atal Pension Yojana (APY): For salary/income earners and small self-employed persons aged 18 to 40 years. The subscriber chooses a pension amount (₹1,000, ₹2,000, ₹3,000, ₹4,000, or ₹5,000 per month) to begin at age 60. The monthly contribution depends on the entry age and the chosen pension: joining early means tiny contributions; joining at 40 means larger contributions. The Government of India guarantees the minimum pension to the subscriber — if investments earn less than promised, the Government covers the difference. Government co-contribution: for subscribers who enrolled in the initial window and are not income-tax payers, the Government contributes 50% of the subscriber's contribution subject to a maximum of ₹1,000 per year (for eligible members). After the subscriber's death, the spouse gets 50% of the pension, and on both lives being gone the accumulated corpus is returned to the nominee. Contributions are auto-debited from the bank/post office account, with missed-payment rules and penalties, so keep some balance in the account. Pradhan Mantri Shram Yogi Maandhan (PM-SYM): A voluntary pension for unorganised workers aged 18-40 years with an income of about ₹15,000 or less per month, who are not covered by EPFO/ESIC or a similar scheme, and who are not income-tax payers. The subscriber contributes a small monthly amount that rises with age — typically ranging from ₹55 per month for a young entrant (age 18) up to ₹200 per month for an entrant at age 40. Two methods are recognised for fixing the SI per hectare, and the State/UT chooses which to apply for each district-crop combination: - **Scale of Finance basis.** The District Level Technical Committee (DLTC), informed by the cost of cultivation, recommends a "Scale of Finance" (the loan eligibility per hectare) for each crop; the State/UTs adopt it. SI per hectare equals the Scale of Finance for the crop, and SI for a farmer = Scale of Finance × the notified/insured area sown under the crop. - **Value of Notional Average Yield basis.** Alternatively, the SI may be fixed as the Notional Average Yield (NAY) of the crop in the district multiplied by the Minimum Support Price (MSP) of the current year; where no MSP is declared, the farm-gate price notified by the marketing department/board is used. The actual yield of the season is estimated through Crop Cutting Experiments (CCEs) and, increasingly, technology-based methods such as YES-TECH, remote sensing and drones. For indemnity calculation the State also fixes an **indemnity level** (70%, 80% or 90%) per crop, and the **Threshold Yield (TY) = Average/Normal Yield × Indemnity level**. The yield-based claim formula is: > Claim = (Threshold Yield − Actual Yield) ÷ Threshold Yield × Sum Insured So a higher threshold yield or a larger Sum Insured increases the indemnity payable when yield falls. The premium is charged on the Sum Insured, and the actuarial/bidded premium rate applied to the SI determines the total premium for the season. Since the scheme's revision, the earlier practice of capping the Sum Insured (which used to shrink the insured value) has been removed, so farmers are indemnified against the full Sum Insured fixed for their notified crop and area. The State notification, tender documents and the National Crop Insurance Portal (NCIP) record the SI per hectare for every notified crop and district. ## 3. Who Is Eligible

Short-term crop loans (KCC-linked) Short-term crop loans are working-capital loans for one cropping season. Their purpose is to meet the cash and kind expenses of cultivation — seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, hired labour, irrigation charges, machinery hire and the family's basic needs during the season — so that the farmer can grow the crop without selling assets or borrowing from informal money-lenders. The main instrument is the Kisan Credit Card (KCC), a revolving credit facility introduced in 1998 and operated through the cooperative channel by PACS and cooperative banks. Salient features: - The credit limit is fixed from the *scale of finance* — the district-level notified per-hectare cost of cultivation for each crop — multiplied by the area the farmer will sow, plus 10% of that amount as contingency for price/cost changes. - The KCC limit also covers post-harvest storage and the household's consumption needs; the consumption component is capped at about 10% of the credit limit. - The card is valid for a fixed term (commonly five years) and is reviewed/renewed yearly; it is revolving, so once the member repays, the money can be drawn again without a fresh application. - Because scale of finance depends on the crop, soil, irrigation and the district, the loan amount varies by farmer and area. Insurance Basics for Farming Households Insurance (bima) exists to protect a family from a sudden financial shock — the death of the earner, an accident, or crop failure. Every farming household should understand the difference between life insurance and general insurance, and should know the cheap government schemes that provide a basic safety net. Life insurance: pays the nominated family a fixed sum when the life insured passes away. Choosing a term (pure protection) life policy is cheaper than a savings-linked policy; the national government schemes below are the most affordable entry point. Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) — life cover: For an annual premium of ₹436 per year, the family member nominated by the subscriber gets ₹2,00,000 on the death of the insured (from any cause, subject to policy terms). Enrolment is open to people aged 18-50 years with a savings account. The premium is auto-debited every year, and the scheme is available through banks and cooperative institutions; one rupee of premium (₹436) buys several lakh of a poorest-household financial cover. Claims are paid to the nominee on submission of the death certificate and policy documents. Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) — accident cover: For a very small annual premium of ₹20 per year, the insured is covered for accidental death and total permanent disability up to ₹2,00,000 and partial permanent disability (loss of one limb or eye, etc.) up to ₹1,00,000. Who Is Eligible All farmers growing notified crops in notified areas are eligible to insure — there is no landholding limit, and no distinction by category. Concretely: - **Loanee farmers.** Farmers who have availed a short-term crop loan or Kisan Credit Card (KCC) for a notified crop from a bank/financial institution. Their enrolment is handled by the lending branch, and the premium is ordinarily debited to the loan account. With effect from Kharif 2020 the scheme is **voluntary for everyone, including loanees**; a loanee farmer who does not wish to be covered must submit a written declaration/opting-out form to the bank branch at least 7 days before the season's cut-off date, failing which the farmer is deemed covered. A farmer whose KCC/crop loan has turned **sub-standard** is not treated as a loanee for the scheme (the bank may still help such a farmer enrol as a non-loanee). - **Non-loanee farmers.** All other farmers — small, marginal, large, and those who do not take crop loans — may enrol voluntarily through the prescribed channels (Common Service Centres, insurance company offices/agents, the crop insurance portal/app, and State-level facilitation centres, e.g. Rythu Bharosa Kendras in some States). - **Sharecroppers and tenant farmers.** Expressly eligible. They must hold an insurable interest in the insured crop/land and submit State-recognised documentary proof — Records of Rights (RoR), Land Possession Certificate (LPC) or a valid tenancy contract/agreement/cultivation certificate as permitted by the State notification — because their name may not appear on the revenue

# Cooperative and Rural Grievance Redressal in India ## 1. Cooperative Dispute Escalation Ladder Cooperative grievance redressal in India runs along two parallel tracks, and the very first step is to identify which one applies to your society. If the society is a **multi-State cooperative society** (members operating in more than one State) it is governed by the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 and the **Central Registrar** (Office of the Registrar of Co-operative Societies, Ministry of Co-operation, New Delhi) has jurisdiction. Every other society — including nearly all Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), Village Service Societies, and district/State-level cooperatives — is registered under the Cooperative Societies Act of its own State and falls under that **State's Registrar of Cooperative Societies**. It is the registration, not the member's residence, that decides the forum. The standard escalation ladder for a member is: - **Step 1 – Member to society management (PACS/general body level):** lodge a written complaint with the secretary/manager, record it in the society's complaint (shikayat) register, and meet the chairman or the managing committee/board of directors. Keep a dated copy with an acknowledgement. - **Step 2 – Board / Managing Committee:** if the day-to-day management does not act, raise the matter before the board, whose powers include rectifying accounts, refunding deposits, correcting dividends, and issuing loan statements. - **Step 3 – General Body / Annual General Meeting (AGM):** the general body is the supreme authority of the society. Every member has a right to raise a grievance at the AGM, inspect accounts and registers, and move a resolution. Unresolved issues raised here create an official record that strengthens a later complaint. - **Step 4 – Registrar of Cooperative Societies:** the member files a written complaint with the State Registrar's office (or the district/assistant registrar/inspector). Digital Payments for Rural Users (UPI and Safety) UPI (Unified Payments Interface) is a free, 24×7 system built by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) that lets a person send and receive money instantly using a mobile number-linked virtual payment address (VPA), bank account plus IFSC, QR code, or the recipient's UPI ID, without giving their bank account number to the sender. Money moves directly between bank accounts; no cash and no cheques are needed. To use UPI you need a smartphone, a bank account, and a registered mobile number; you create a UPI PIN (a secret password chosen by you) inside your bank's UPI app. UPI works person-to-person, from your phone to any merchant's QR code, and even voice-based in some systems. Three absolute safety rules: 1. Never share your UPI PIN, ATM PIN, OTP, CVV, or full card number with anyone — not with a relative, a "bank employee", a "bank official", a "government officer", or anyone who calls claiming you have won a prize. The 2020 farm-sector reforms (the Farmers' Produce Trade and Commerce (Promotion and Facilitation) Act, 2020 and the Farmers (Empowerment and Protection) Agreement on Price Assurance and Farm Services Act, 2020 — sometimes referred to together as the farmers' produce/trade reform laws) were enacted to widen marketing options for farmers, including through electronic trading and contract-based price assurance. These 2020 enactments were subsequently repealed with effect from December 2021 and are no longer in force; therefore current agriculture marketing arrangements continue to operate through the existing APMC/Mandi framework and cooperative channels. The general purpose of producer organisations — whether cooperative or FPO route — remains to give farmer members collective bargaining strength, better access to credit, inputs, processing and markets, and a fair share of the final price. # Ministry of Cooperation — Schemes and Support for Cooperatives in India The Ministry of Cooperation was created on 6 July 2021 by transferring cooperation-related subjects from the erstwhile Ministry of Agriculture, Cooperation and Farmers Welfare. It works on the vision of "Sahakar se Samriddhi" (prosperity through cooperation). The Ministry's principal agencies include the National Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC), the National Council for Cooperative Training (NCCT), the National Cooperative Union of India (NCUI), the Central Registrar of Cooperative Societies, and, in the credit and development field, NABARD. Scheme finance reaches primary cooperative societies mainly through NCDC (term/investment loans and some grants) and through NABARD-linked credit lines, while education and training are delivered through NCCT institutes and State Cooperative Unions. This document summarises the principal Ministry-level schemes, the training ecosystem, and the routes by which cooperative societies access finance. ## Sahakar Mitra — NCDC Internship Scheme (2020) Sahakar Mitra: Scheme on Internship Programme (SIP) is an internship initiative of the National Cooperative Development Corporation (NCDC). It was launched in June 2020, initially under the administrative oversight of the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare and, since the creation of the Ministry of Cooperation in 2021, is associated with the cooperative development portfolio of that Ministry. The objective of the scheme is to connect young people — school, university and college students and recent professional graduates — with the working of the cooperative sector, so that interns gain practical field experience while cooperative institutions access new and innovative ideas from young professionals. NCDC coordinates the placement of interns, provides the stipend from its earmarked funds, and monitors the internships through its regional offices. Key features that have been officially published:

Unresolved issues raised here create an official record that strengthens a later complaint. - **Step 4 – Registrar of Cooperative Societies:** the member files a written complaint with the State Registrar's office (or the district/assistant registrar/inspector). The Registrar can order an **inquiry**, an **inspection**, an **audit**, or **surcharge proceedings** against officials who misappropriated funds, and can direct the society to comply with bye-laws. - **Step 5 – Dispute reference and arbitration:** most State Acts let a member refer a "dispute" (touching the constitution, management or business of the society) to the Registrar, who may decide it himself or refer it to arbitration. The award is enforced as if it were a decree of a civil court. - **Step 6 – Cooperative Tribunal / appellate authority and courts:** appeals against Registrar orders or awards go to the appellate body named in the State Act (a Cooperative Tribunal or appellate Registrar; in many States the District Judge hears such appeals). Civil suits are generally excluded for matters that must go through the Act's own machinery, but a limited remedy exists by way of writ under Articles 226/227 of the Constitution where the process is illegal or against natural justice. For multi-State societies the route is compressed: dispute to arbitration by an arbitrator appointed by the Central Registrar (Section 84), member complaints on deposits and member rights to the Co-operative Ombudsman (Section 85A), and civil courts are largely barred (Section 117). Savings / fixed deposits at PACS Apart from lending, a PACS mobilises savings from its members, and this deposit base, together with share capital and borrowings, funds the society's lending. Most societies offer: - A savings (passbook) account, where members can deposit and withdraw small amounts at any time. - Term/ fixed deposits (FD) and recurring deposits, where money is locked for a fixed period and earns a higher rate. - In many states the society also accepts deposits from non-members, but the main product is the member savings account. Features of PACS deposits: - Interest rates are not fixed by any single central rule — each society's board fixes its rates in the by-laws, within state cooperative-deposit norms. Rates therefore *vary by society*, and a PACS may pay more or less than a commercial bank. The rate on fixed deposits is usually higher than the savings rate. - There is no universal deposit insurance for society deposits: deposit insurance under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) covers commercial and cooperative *banks*, but PACS deposits are generally not covered by DICGC. Some states have their own guarantee or proposal under discussion, so a member should check the position in their state and by-laws. - Withdrawals from savings are allowed as per the society's rules (usually a withdrawal slip signed by the account holder), subject to the account holder's KYC documents. Fixed deposits can generally be withdrawn before maturity only on the society's penal terms, which also vary by

rdance with co-operative principles, or, after 2023, where registration was obtained by misrepresentation, false information or fraud (section 86(2)). A society may resolve to wind itself up by a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, in which case the Central Registrar shall order it (section 86(6)). Multi-State co-operative banks cannot be wound up without the Reserve Bank's sanction and the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 applies to their winding up (sections 86(5), 87); the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation is reimbursed where it has paid depositors (section 88). Liquidation. On the winding-up order the Central Registrar appoints a liquidator (section 89), in whom all assets vest; he takes custody of the property, realises it by sale, sues and defends, assesses contributions (including debts and liquidation costs) payable by members, past members, deceased members' estates and former officers, investigates and pays claims in order of priority, makes compromises, carries on the business so far as beneficial, and disposes of surplus assets — per the bye-laws' designated purpose or, if none, to the members with the previous sanction of the Central Government (sections 90–91). Contributions assessed by the liquidator rank next to sums due to the Central or State Government or a local authority (section 92). A winding-up order is appealable (section 99). On the liquidator's report, the Central Registrar cancels the registration and the society stands dissolved (section 93). ## 9. Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) — accident cover: For a very small annual premium of ₹20 per year, the insured is covered for accidental death and total permanent disability up to ₹2,00,000 and partial permanent disability (loss of one limb or eye, etc.) up to ₹1,00,000. Persons aged 18-70 years holding a savings or Post Office account can join, with annual auto-debit renewal. This is accident-only cover; it does not pay on natural death. Crop insurance — Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY): protects the crop itself. Farmers pay a low, fixed share of the sum insured (2% of the sum insured for kharif foodgrain/oilseed crops, 1.5% for rabi foodgrain/oilseed crops, and 5% for annual commercial/horticultural crops); the Government of India pays the balance premium. The sum insured is based on the cost of cultivation per hectare (scale of finance) notified by state governments, so the maximum claim equals the full cost of growing the crop. PMFBY covers prevented sowing, standing crop loss due to non-preventable natural risks, post-harvest losses, localized calamities such as hailstorms, and add-ons notified by states. Claims are assessed through crop-cutting experiments (CCEs). Enrolment happens before notified cut-off dates for each season, so farmers must enrol in time and keep the premium receipt. General rules: keep the nominee's name updated on every policy, keep policy papers and receipts safe, inform the insurer immediately on any event, file claims within the notified deadlines, and never buy insurance purely as an investment without understanding returns. Read the policy document to know what is covered and what is excluded. ## 6. Pension Schemes (Budhapa Suraksha) A pension is a fixed monthly payment after a person stops working. Document Checklist for Claims Farmers should keep the following in hand — the exact list is mostly relevant to localized-calimity, post-harvest and prevented-sowing claims, since widespread yield claims require no form: 1. **Intimation / claim form.** Duly filled and signed claim form with the crop, season, and area details; if information is not fully available at the time of loss, a semi-filled form may be lodged and the completed form submitted within 7 days of the loss. 2. **Land record / proof of cultivation.** RoR, Land Possession Certificate, or the tenancy agreement/cultivation certificate (for sharecroppers/tenant farmers) proving insurable interest. 3. **Sowing certificate / sowing declaration.** Sowing certificate or the crop/area declaration recorded on the portal (or the bank loan/sowing details for loanees), confirming the crop actually sown as insured. 4. **Premium receipt / policy evidence.** The enrolment acknowledgment, premium-payment receipt or policy number showing the premium was remitted before the cut-off date. 5. **Bank account details.** Aadhaar-seeded bank passbook/cancelled cheque details for claim DBT. 6. **Evidence of the calamity event.** Local newspaper cutting and any other available photographic evidence (preferably geo-tagged farm photos) substantiating the occurrence and severity of the hailstorm/landslide/flood/unseasonal-rain event. 7. **Survey / CCE report.** The joint survey report of the loss assessor and block agriculture officer (localized/post-harvest), or the CCE-based yield report / claim-calculation statement (widespread claims). 8. **Supporting loan documents (loanees).** KCC/crop-loan sanction details and the statement from the bank showing the premium debit. RTI — Right to Information Act, 2005 The RTI Act gives every citizen the right to access information held by, or under the control of, a **public authority** – to inspect records and books, take notes and certified copies, and obtain certified samples of material. A "public authority" (Section 2(h)) means any body established, constituted, owned, controlled or **substantially financed, directly or indirectly, by the appropriate Government**. **Using RTI for cooperative matters.** A cooperative society itself is usually a membership body and not a public authority merely because it is co-operatively regulated – but the *public* offices that hold records around a society or scheme are: the office of the **Registrar of Cooperative Societies** (registration file, audit reports, inquiry/inspection reports, action on complaints); Government financing agencies and public banks (subsidy, DBT, KCC disbursal); NABARD-controlled institutions; the agriculture department and **PMFBY** desks (notifications, expected yields, claim computations, crop-cutting experiment records); and public-sector insurers. Ask specifically for copies of documents – e.g., "certified copy of the audit report of society X for 2023-24" or "details of PMFBY claim amount and its disbursement under policy no. Y." **How to file.** Send a written application (in English, Hindi or the local language; electronic filing is allowed) to the **Central/State Public Information Officer (CPIO/SPIO)** of the specific department. You may file online on many State RTI portals or the central `rtionline.gov.in` portal. You **need not give a reason** for asking; you need only give contact details. Fee is generally **₹10** per application (Central rules; States set their own, usually ₹10; fee is waived for Below-Poverty-Line applicants – any citizen can make an application but BPL pay no fee under the Central rules). The Ombudsman must complete the inquiry and adjudication **within three months**, may issue directions which the society must comply with within one month, and possesses the powers of a civil court (summoning witnesses, examining them on oath, discovery and production of books). A society aggrieved by the directions may appeal to the Central Registrar within one month, and the Registrar decides in **forty-five days**; his decision is final and binding. **Mediation and settlement.** Section 84(5) imports the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, whose philosophy, post-2015 reforms and the Mediation Act, 2023 encourage the parties to attempt conciliation/mediation before and during arbitration. A member can also raise and settle genuine grievances through the society's own general body before any formal reference. **Civil court exclusion and enforcement.** The award/decision of the arbitrator is executable as if it were a decree of a civil court (Chapter XI, Sections 94–98). Section 117 bars courts from questioning decisions or orders made under the Act except as the Act itself provides, and civil suits are not maintainable where the Act's machinery applies. # PACS Services — Primary Agricultural Credit Society This guide explains what a Primary Agricultural Credit Society (PACS) is and what services it offers to rural farmers and members in India. It covers the society's structure and membership, crop loans under the Kisan Credit Card (KCC), long-term loans, savings and deposits, sale of agricultural inputs, disbursement of government schemes, share capital and loan limits, loan recovery and default rules, and the digitisation ("smart PACS") programme under NABARD. Exact interest rates and charges set by individual societies vary by state and by-laws; where a Government of India scheme fixes a figure, that figure is stated. ## 1. What is a PACS — structure, membership and role A PACS is the village-level grassroots unit of India's cooperative credit system. It is a cooperative society of farmers and rural residents registered under the State Cooperative Societies Act of the state in which it operates (multi-state societies register under the Multi-State Cooperative Societies Act, 2002, as amended in 2023). Each PACS has a defined area of operation — normally one village or a cluster of villages — and is administered by its own elected board under the supervision of the Registrar of Cooperative Societies (RCS) of the state. A PACS is not a bank, but it lends to farmers using funds it raises through member share capital, deposits and borrowing from the district and state cooperative banks. The short-term cooperative credit structure (STCCS) is three-tier: - Tier 1 — PACS at the village level, which lend directly to farmers. - Tier 2 — District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs), which hold the dealings and lending limits of PACS, provide funds to them and supervise their day-to-day working. - Tier 3 — State Cooperative Banks (SCBs, the "apex" banks), which sit at the head of the structure, link it to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and obtain refinance from NABARD. What counts as default: an instalment or repayment amount left unpaid after its due date. On default the society: - Adds overdue interest/penalty as per the by-laws and policy — the overdue rate and grace period vary by society. - Stops or restricts fresh lending to the defaulter until the account is regularised. - Reports the account as non-performing/overdue under the applicable state and NABARD norms, which affects the member's future borrowing. Personal contact — the secretary or the recovery staff/officer discusses the account, offers instalment options, and tries to resolve the matter voluntarily before harsher steps. 3. Legal steps under the Cooperative Societies Act — where a debt remains unpaid, the society may refer the matter to arbitration/the Registrar and obtain an award or recovery certificate. The certificate can then be executed by recovery machinery: attachment and auction of the secured/mortgaged property after due process, or set-off against the member's deposits, as the by-laws and law allow. 4. Guarantors — the surety becomes liable to the extent of the guarantee. No-harassment rules: recovery must be lawful and orderly. Neither cooperative law nor RBI/cooperative fair-practice norms permit recovery through humiliation, force, wrongful detention, or seizure of the bare essentials of a rural household or productive stock beyond the secured property. A borrower facing harsh or unlawful recovery can complain to the society board, the DCCB, the Registrar of Cooperative Societies, or the district cooperative office, and can ask for a resettlement/instalment plan.

# Financial Literacy for Rural Farming Households in India Practical money knowledge for Indian farmers and cooperative members: interest (byaj), EMIs (kist), savings (bachat), insurance (bima), pension, borrowing choices, government schemes, digital payments, and credit scores (CIBIL). Every farmer should understand at least the basics before taking any loan or investment decision. These notes are general guidance; always confirm current rates and rules with your bank, cooperative society (sahakari samiti), PACS, or the scheme's official website. ## 1. Simple Interest (Sadharan Byaj) Simple interest is the easiest way to calculate the cost of a loan or the return on a deposit. You pay (or earn) interest only on the original amount borrowed or saved, called the principal (mul dhan), for the whole period. The interest does not grow by itself. The formula is: **Simple Interest (SI) = (P × R × T) / 100**, where P is the principal in rupees, R is the annual interest rate in percent, and T is the time in years. The total amount to be repaid or received at the end is **A = P + SI**. Worked rural example: A farmer takes a crop loan (karj/rin) of ₹50,000 at an annual interest rate of 7% for 1 year. SI = (50,000 × 7 × 1) / 100 = ₹3,500. So the farmer repays ₹53,500 in total — the original ₹50,000 plus ₹3,500 interest. If the same ₹50,000 is kept in a deposit earning 7% simple interest for 1 year, the depositor earns ₹3,500 interest and receives ₹53,500 at maturity. Simple interest logic applies to many short-term rural transactions: small loans within a cooperative society, arrears on loan recovery, and deposits where interest is paid out each year rather than added to the principal. Because interest is calculated on the original principal only, the total interest bill stays predictable and does not compound. Practical points for a farmer: - Always write down the principal, the agreed rate (byaj dar), and the loan period before signing; confirm whether the rate is per

Document Checklist Before Complaining Preparing a complete file before complaining decides whether the grievance is taken seriously. Assemble originals and keep clean photocopies: **Identity and membership:** Aadhaar, voter ID/passport, farmer identity card/Kisan Credit Card booklet, membership passbook of the PACS/society, society registration number, and spouse/family details if the holding is joint. **Loan and banking papers:** KCC card and sanction letter, loan application and agreement, passbook showing premium/loan entries, EMI repayment receipts, loan account statements, bank's written replies (or their absence), and any notice of default/recovery. **Insurance and crop documents:** PMFBY policy/cover note with policy number and notified insurance unit, premium receipt (farmer's share) and the portal acknowledgment, season notification (crop, notified area, sum insured), sowing certificate/deed and sown-area declaration, crop-cutting experiment (CCE) records and yield data, and certificate of loss from patwari/DLMC where available. **Evidence of loss:** date-stamped mobile photos and videos of the crop at the time of each event (sowing/germination failure, flood, drought, hail, pest attack, post-harvest loss), GPS/geo-tag data, **FIR** (if applicable – e.g., crop theft, fire, or damage in a riot/calamity where a police report is relevant), panchnama/spot inspection notes, and statements of eyewitness neighbours. **Procedural proofs:** the date-stamped complaint letters to the society/Registrar/insurer/RBI ombudsman/PMFBY portal, acknowledgement/diary numbers, email/SMS records, reply letters

Written and dated at every step.** Always complain in writing; never rely on phone calls. Missing a deadline can bar the remedy entirely. **5. Quantify and be precise.** State the exact amount claimed, the dates of each loss event, and the specific relief asked. Ambiguous demands ("do something") are parked at the bottom of the pile; a precise prayer gets a precise reply. **6. Chase, escalate, and use free forums.** Follow up in writing at each stage and escalate promptly up the ladder. Use the no-fee machinery – Banking/Insurance Ombudsmen, PMFBY portal, Lok Adalat, free legal aid (helpline 15100) – before spending money on counsel. For cooperative money disputes, Lok Adalat or arbitration is usually faster than a civil suit that the Act may bar anyway. **7. It has been reasonably proven that satellite based vegetation indices (such as, Normalized Difference Vegetation Index, NDVI and Normalized Difference Wetness Index, NDWI) can help in demarcating the cropped areas into clusters on the basis of crop health . This feature can be successfully used to target the CCEs within the Insurance Unit (IU). In other words, satellite imagery can help in ‘smart sampling’ (stratified sampling) of CCEs. This will help in optimizing the number of CCEs, to make them representative of different crop conditions. This is expected to reduce the total need of CCEs by about 30-40% while maintaining similar accuracy . It will also give a more representative yield of the IU, as it will consider all crop pixels (fields) within the IU an d not just location of 4 CCEs. States can adopt this technique (of using satellite based remote sensing data for planning of Crop Cutting Experiments) in generating yield estimates while following digital protocol outlined in the preceding paragraphs. For using satellite data for smart sampling, there is a need to generate specific crop map. MNCFC under the FASAL project of the DAC&FW prepares crop maps for various crops, as mentioned in Section 25, para 25.4. These crop maps can be used for CCE planning. Vegetation Indices (NDVI and NWDI) need to be computed for the cropped area. On the basis of Vegetation Index, the crop area can be categorized into poor, medium, good and very good crop health strata. Within each stratum, CCE points should be selected randomly. Additionally, ground truthing within these IUs can be done in order to develop crop yield model to ascertain yield estimation of the crop and simultaneously can act as a reconciliation/verification tool of actual CCEs conducted on the field. This can be done in consultation with MNCFC, NRSC (ISRO), SAC (ISRO), SRSC and IASRI. DBT removes middlemen, reduces leakage, and delivers money faster to the right person. Panels of serving/retired judges, lawyers and social workers hear parties and effect **conciliation-based settlements**; recovery of small loan amounts, compensation, and money claims are frequent subject matter. This makes Lok Adalat an attractive, free, quick settlement forum for many rural cooperative and banking money disputes before rushing to court. ## 7. Multi-State Co-operative Society The central jurisdictional divide in Indian co-operative law is between a society registered under a State Co-operative Societies Act and one registered under the MSCS Act, 2002. Legislative competence. Co-operative societies other than multi-State societies fall within Entry 32, List II (State List), and Part IXB does not bind purely State societies after Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021) 11 SCC 633. Multi-State co-operative societies, having objects not confined to one State, fall within Entry 44, List I (Union List), are governed by the MSCS Act, 2002, and Part IXB applies through Article 243ZR. Registration authority. A State society is registered by the Registrar of Co-operative Societies of its State, under that State's Act, with jurisdiction confined to that State. A multi-State society is registered by the Central Registrar, can admit members and do business across States, and is a body corporate under Central law. Membership geography. A State society's members and area of operation lie within one State; a multi-State society's main objects must serve members in more than one State, and an all-individual society needs at least fifty members from each of two or more States (section 6(2)). Supervision and audit. State societies are audited, inspected and supervised by the State Registrar; multi-State societies are audited annually by chartered accountants under sections 70–77 and are open to inquiry, inspection and special audit by the Central Registrar and Central Government. Government nominees on the board follow shareholding thresholds (section 48), as in State Acts. Dispute resolution. Disputes touching the constitution or business of a multi-State society, other than those before authorities under the Act, can be referred to arbitration before the Central Registrar (section 84); his decisions and orders are executed like civil-court decrees (section 94). Share capital, membership fees and loan limit Becoming a member: a person applies to the society in the prescribed form, pays a small admission/membership fee, and buys the minimum number of shares fixed by the by-laws. Share values are set in the by-laws and *vary by society* — a common pattern is a modest per-share value with a requirement of one to a few shares — and a member may buy more shares to raise the qualifying share capital. Whatever the shares, one member has one vote. Share capital is the society's own (owned) fund. It is not a deposit: it stays as the member's capital stake, earns a dividend only if the society makes a profit and declares it (subject to statutory reserves and the by-laws), and is refundable on leaving the society as per the by-laws, normally after settling all dues. The society's share capital is one of the bases on which the DCCB sanctions the society's overall borrowing limit. Loan limit: the board fixes each member's borrowing limit. It is not a fixed all-India figure; it is computed per member from: - Repayment capacity — net farm and family income after essential family expenses. - Landholding and the area actually cropped, applied against the notified scale of finance for the crops grown. - The member's share capital/owned contribution and the security available. - Past repayment record — a clean repayer gets a higher limit; a defaulter is reduced. - For KCC loans, the formula is scale of finance × cropped area, plus 10% contingency, plus the household consumption component (up to about 10% of the credit

How a rural user can build and protect the score: - Take a small formal loan (KCC, MUDRA Shishu, gold loan, or a first vehicle loan) and repay every instalment on time. - Never miss the interest payment on a crop loan; even one delay gets recorded and repeated delays push the score down. - If a payment is late, pay as soon as possible rather than ignoring it — longer overdue periods damage the score more. - Avoid taking more credit than needed; high monthly obligations make approval harder. - Check your free credit report (every credit bureau must give one free report a year) and point out any error to the bureau. Consequences of default: defaulting on a loan — failing to repay as agreed — lowers the score for years, marks the report with the default, and leads the lender to refuse future credit or offer it only at a high rate. Beyond the score, the lender can take recovery action: notices, recalling the loan, and for secured loans (like a gold or land mortgage loan from a bank or cooperative), legal recovery under laws such as SARFAESI, and cooperative societies may recover dues under the Cooperative Societies Act through the Registrar. A guarantor also stands to be affected if the borrower defaults. Default is not a personal tragedy to be ashamed of — a farmer hit by crop failure should go to the lender quickly, discuss restructuring or rescheduling of the loan, and use every formal channel rather than hiding the problem, because hiding it makes the score and the recovery problem worse.

# PMFBY Operational Details (फसल बीमा / Fasal Bima) Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY / पीएमएफबीवाई) is the Government of India's crop-insurance / fasal bima scheme, implemented by the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare and delivered through empanelled insurance companies (ICs) with support from banks, State Governments/UTs and the District / State administration. Coverage is **area based** for widespread yield losses and **individual farm based** for localized calamities and post-harvest losses. This document covers the operational mechanics: what is covered, how the Sum Insured and premium are fixed, who can enrol, the enrolment and claims process, claim documents, common rejection grounds, grievance routes and the principal changes brought in by the revised (PMFBY 2.0 / Kharif-2020) guidelines. Premium figures here are only a recap of the rates fixed by Government; refer to the scheme guidelines for the full legal text. ## 1. What PMFBY Covers PMFBY insures notified crops grown in notified areas against a comprehensive set of non-preventable natural risks — from before sowing to the post-harvest stage. The State Government/UT notifies, for each season (Kharif and Rabi), the crops and the insurance units (typically districts, sub-districts or villages) to be covered, along with indemnity levels; only crops and areas appearing in that notification are insurable. - **Standing crop / yield loss (basic cover).** Loss to the standing crop from sowing to harvesting due to non-preventable risks such as drought, dry spells, flood, inundation, wide-spread pest and disease attack, landslide, storm, hailstorm, cyclone and natural fire due to lightning. This is the core cover, assessed on an area-approach basis using crop yield data, and compensates the shortfall between the threshold yield and the actual yield of the season. - **Prevented sowing / planting / germination.** When farmers who intended to sow a notified crop (and incurred preparatory expenses) are

Registrar of Cooperative Societies The Registrar of Cooperative Societies (RCS) is the senior State officer appointed under the State Cooperative Societies Act who supervises every cooperative registered in that State. Key functions of the Registrar: - **Registration and governance:** registering new societies, approving bye-laws and their amendments, supervising elections, and receiving copies of AGM minutes and annual accounts. - **Audit and accounts:** ordering the statutory audit of societies, since the Registrar fixes the audit of every society's accounts each year. - **Inquiry, inspection and investigation:** on complaint or suo moto, ordering an inquiry into the constitution, working and financial condition of a society, inspecting books and records (including the books of an indebted society), and appointing a committee to investigate serious irregularities. - **Disciplinary and recovery powers:** conducting inquiry and issuing surcharge certificates to recover misappropriated amounts from defaulting office-bearers, directing repayment of loans, and ordering the supersession or winding up of a failed society and appointment of an administrator/liquidator. - **Dispute resolution:** receiving references of members' disputes and proceeding with conciliation, decision or arbitration under the Act. Recurring Deposit (RD): deposit a fixed small amount every month for a fixed period (commonly 6 months to 10 years). Helps build a lump sum through discipline; interest generally higher than a savings account; rates vary by bank and duration. Ideal for a farmer saving a fixed monthly amount towards a goal such as a tractor tyre, festival, or school fees. Fixed Deposit (FD): deposit a lump sum once for a fixed term (e.g., 1, 3, or 5 years). Attracts a higher interest rate than savings/RD; rates vary by bank, amount, and tenure. Senior citizens (60+ years) usually get a slightly higher rate; some banks offer tax-saving FDs of 5 years. Money is locked until maturity, though premature withdrawal is often allowed with a penalty. FDs up to ₹5,00,000 per depositor per bank are protected by DICGC deposit insurance. Public Provident Fund (PPF): a 15-year government-backed investment available at banks and post offices. Interest is set by the Government of India and announced quarterly; in recent years it has generally stayed in the 7-8% band. Deposits are eligible for income-tax deduction under Section 80C, and the accumulated amount with interest is tax-free. Loans can be taken against it from the 3rd year. Compound interest applies. Best for long-term goals like retirement planning. Post Office savings: the Post Office offers a savings account, RD, FD (Time Deposit), National Savings Certificate (NSC), PPF, Monthly Income Scheme (MIS, paying a monthly interest-like payout on a lump sum), and Senior Citizen Savings Scheme (SCSS) for 60+. These are backed by the Government of India (sovereign security), available even in small towns, and require low amounts to start. Rates vary and are announced by the government. Rule of thumb: keep emergency money (3-6 months of household expenses) in savings/RD; park medium-term money in FD or Post Office MIS; invest for long-term goals in PPF or SCSS. ##

What Makes a Complaint Strong A strong complaint is one a forum can act on quickly. Seven rules matter in practice: **1. Evidence before narrative.** Photocopy everything, keep originals, date every document, and lead with the strongest proof – a receipt, bank statement, policy, CCE record or written reply defeats arguments. A photo without a date, or a claim without the premium receipt, rarely moves the inspector or ombudsman. **2. Correct forum, correct claim.** Match the grievance to the jurisdiction: a multi-State society dispute to arbitration under the MSCS Act; a state society to the State Registrar; a banking deficiency to the bank and then the Banking Ombudsman (only for covered banks); an insurer's denial to the insurer's GRO then Insurance Ombudsman; an information gap to RTI. The Chairperson must have held the post of Additional Secretary to the Government of India or equivalent rank, the Vice-Chairperson Joint Secretary rank; members need the prescribed qualifications. Members serve three years or until age sixty-five, whichever is earlier, and are re-appointable. Conduct of elections. Elections of board members are conducted in the general meeting by secret ballot, in the prescribed manner (section 45J). The term of elected board members and office bearers is five years from the date of election, office bearers' terms being co-terminus with the board. Casual vacancies can be filled by nomination from the same class of members, but only up to one-third of the elected directors and only when less than half the board's original term remains; vacancies beyond one-third must be filled by election. The Chairperson and Chief Executive must inform the Authority at least six months before the board's term expires, and the society must provide the Authority the infrastructure, personnel, documents and funds needed. Elections must be held before the term expires. The Authority appoints Returning Officers and Assistant Returning Officers (section 45K), appoints observers to supervise polls, and may issue directions — binding on the board, its members, the Chief Executive and staff — for free and fair elections (section 45L). Election expenses are borne by the society. The Chairperson and Vice-Chairperson (President and Vice-President) are elected by the board from amongst its elected members per the Authority's directions, and the Chief Executive issues the certificate of election after the resolution is concluded (section 49(2)(aa)).

Because interest is calculated on the original principal only, the total interest bill stays predictable and does not compound. Practical points for a farmer: - Always write down the principal, the agreed rate (byaj dar), and the loan period before signing; confirm whether the rate is per annum. - Check whether interest is simple or compound — this can change the total cost significantly on long loans. - Interest is usually charged on the daily or monthly outstanding balance in formal institutions; repaying early reduces the days for which interest is charged. - In cooperative societies and PACS, loan terms are set by the board under rules approved by the Registrar; ask for the loan document (rin patra) and repayment schedule. Simple interest is rare for long-term institutional loans because compounding is more common (see the next topic), but the simple-interest calculation remains the foundation for understanding every other interest concept in banking. ## 2. Compound Interest (Chakravridhi Byaj) Compound interest means interest is added to the principal at the end of each period, and the next period's interest is calculated on the new, larger total. This is called "interest on interest" — with time, growth becomes faster and faster. The formula is **A = P × (1 + r)^t**, where A is the final amount, P the principal, r the annual rate as a decimal (e.g., 7% = 0.07), and t the number of years. Compound interest earned is **CI = A − P**. A simple 5-year example using the same numbers as the simple-interest example: ₹50,000 at 7% compound interest annually. ## 3. EMI Basics (Kist) EMI stands for Equated Monthly Instalment — the fixed amount a borrower pays to a bank or cooperative every month until a loan is fully repaid. The EMI includes both parts of repayment: repayment of a portion of the principal (loan amount) and payment of interest that has accrued. Even though the EMI amount stays the same every month, the split inside it changes as the loan progresses. The standard formula banks and cooperative institutions use is **EMI = P × r × (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n − 1)**, where P is the loan principal, r is the monthly interest rate (annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100), and n is the number of monthly instalments. Illustrative example (learning exercise, not a current bank rate): a loan of ₹1,00,000 at 12% annual interest. Monthly rate = 1%. Over 12 months, the EMI is about ₹8,886. In the first month, interest is 1,00,000 × 1% = ₹1,000, so only about ₹7,886 reduces the principal. Over time the interest portion keeps shrinking and the principal portion keeps growing, until the last instalment is almost entirely principal. This is why a borrower pays much more interest in the early years of a long loan. The critical rule for farmers: **a longer tenure means a lower EMI but a higher total interest cost; a shorter tenure means a higher EMI but less total interest paid.** In the same ₹1,00,000 example at 12%, stretching the loan to 24 months reduces the EMI to roughly ₹4,708 (nearly half) but pushes total interest from about ₹6,600 to about ₹13,000 — almost double. In other words, choosing a longer period makes monthly pressure (kist ka bojh) lighter but makes the loan costlier overall. Practical guidance: - Choose the shortest tenure you can afford to pay every month; never stretch tenure just to reduce the EMI if extra interest will hurt later. - Pay EMIs before the due date — banks and cooperatives charge penal interest on late kist, and a default is reported and damages your credit score. - If you earn extra income (good harvest,

The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 and Part IXB (Articles 243ZH–243ZT) The Constitution (Ninety-seventh Amendment) Act, 2011 (in force from 15 February 2012) made three changes relevant to co-operatives. First, it amended Article 19(1)(c) so that the right reads: all citizens shall have the right "to form associations or unions or co-operative societies." Citizens thus have a fundamental right to form and join a co-operative society, subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(4). Second, it inserted Article 43B into Part IV (Directive Principles): "The State shall endeavour to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies." Third, it inserted Part IXB, "The Co-operative Societies" (Articles 243ZH–243ZT), a constitutional template for co-operative regulation: - Article 243ZH: definitions, including "Registrar" (Central Registrar for multi-State societies, State Registrar otherwise), "multi-State co-operative society", "board" and "office bearer". - Article 243ZI: the State Legislature may by law provide for the incorporation, regulation and winding up of co-operative societies based on voluntary formation, democratic member-control, member-economic participation and autonomous functioning. - Article 243ZJ: State law must fix the number and term of board members and office bearers — the board cannot exceed twenty-one directors and the term cannot exceed five years — with co-option of up to two expert persons in banking, management, finance or co-operation,

Elections to the Board under the MSCS Act Democracy is guaranteed by one-member-one-vote: every member, including an employee-member, has one vote in the society's affairs (section 31). An employee-member cannot, however, vote in board elections or in general meetings that frame or amend bye-laws. Voting is in person; proxies are prohibited, though an institutional member (a society, the Central or State Government, etc.) votes through a person it nominates or authorises (sections 31–32). Along with these, Junior Training Centres (JTCs) provide foot-level training. Together these form the three-tier cooperative training structure (senior, middle and junior level). Courses offered include: - Higher Diploma in Cooperative Management (HDCM) — a longer programme (about 36 weeks/6 months in some centres; 6-9 months has also been published). - Post Graduate Diploma in Cooperative Business Management — about 9 months. - Cooperative Sector Diploma Programmes — about 12 weeks, focused on sectors such as dairy, handloom, cooperative audit, urban cooperative banks, housing cooperatives, fishery and computer applications. - Certificate Course in Cooperative Management and short training/refresher courses, including accounting and computer application courses. Target audience: managers and secretaries of PACS and other cooperative societies, cooperative employees, elected representatives, and officials of cooperative departments; NABARD-sponsored programmes for PACS managerial staff have also been conducted through NCCT units. The training aims to upskill cooperative personnel in management, accounting, governance and sector-specific business. Member-level education (for ordinary members of cooperative societies) is primarily the domain of NCUI (National Cooperative Union of India) and the State Cooperative Unions, which organise member education, publicity and awareness activities. NCUI, the apex representative body of the cooperative movement (established 1929), also orientates college/university lecturers and coordinates publicity. Each year the All India/National Cooperative Week is observed around 14 to 20 November, commemorating the founding of the cooperative union movement; the Ministry and NCUI carry out public awareness and outreach programmes during this week. However, care should be taken to use well calibrated and validated models and also models should be run in spatial at higher resolutio n, at least 5 km. • Identification of Outliers : All these above analyses can be used to check whether there was any reason for yield deviation as presented in the CCE data. Then a yield proxy map may be prepared. The Yield proxy map can be derived from remo te sensing vegetation indices (single or combination of indices), crop simulation model output, or an integration of various parameters, which are related to crop yield, such as soil, weather (gridded), satellite based products, etc. Whatever, yield proxi es to be used, it is the responsibility of the organization to record documentary evidence (from their or other’s published work) that the yield proxy is related to the particular crop’s yield. Then the IU level yields need to be overlaid on the yield pro xy map. Both yield proxy and CCE yield can be divided into 4 -5 categories (e.g. Very good, Good, Medium, Poor, Very poor). Wherever there is large mismatch between yield proxy and the CCE yield (more than 2 levels), the CCE yield for that IU can be conside red, as outliers. • Computing Yield for the Outliers : For the IUs, where the yield was considered as outlier, the yield may be estimated by developing empirical models (statistically significant) between long -term yield data (at IU level or, if not available, higher administrative level) and weather and remote sensing based index data. Using these models, yield for the concerned year should be estimated. www.pmfby.gov.in Revised Operational Guidelines of PMFBY 36 The final yield can be estimated as a combination of CCE Yield and model estimated. The weightage to be g iven to each estimate will depend upon the quality of each estimate (CCE or Model). Low weightage should be given to CCE not conducted properly (without photograph, geo location, proper sampling plan etc.). Similarly lower weightage to be given model estim ates, if model is statistically not highly significant. Wherever, if the model was not statistically significant the average of estimated yields of adjacent blocks should be used (Note: Each and every case may have specific and special cause related to a p roblem and may not be considered as a reference for any other case.) Each time, the stage of the crop should be given prior importance e.g. 10 mm rainfall at vegetative stage and at harvest or post -harvest stage has different impacts; a small amount rainfall having devastating wind -speed have different impact than high amount of rainfall having calm or no -wind. Objective of the Scheme Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) aims at supporting sustainable production in agriculture sector by way of • Providing financial support to farmers suffering crop loss/damage arising out of unforeseen events • Stabilizing the income of farmers to ensure their continuance in farming • Encouraging farmers to adopt innovative and modern agricultural practices • Ensuring flow of c redit to the agriculture sector which will contribute to food security, crop diversification and enhancing growth and competitiveness of agriculture sector besides p rotecting farmers from production risks. 2. Dispute Resolution Under the MSCS Act, 2002 The Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 (as amended in 2023) contains the complete dispute machinery for multi-State societies. Note the current numbering: the dispute provisions are **Section 84 (Reference of disputes)** and **Section 85 (Limitation)** in Chapter IX, plus **Section 85A (Co-operative Ombudsman)** inserted in 2023. Section 86 in the present Act deals with winding up. **Section 84 – Reference of disputes.** Any dispute "touching the constitution, management or business" of a multi-State society between the classes of persons listed in the Section (members, past members, persons claiming through them; members and the society, its board, officers, employees or liquidators; the society and past boards/officers/employees and their heirs; two or more multi-State societies and their liquidators) **shall be referred to arbitration** – subject to repeated exclusions, the disputes are referred to arbitration. Disputes regarding disciplinary action against a paid employee, and industrial disputes, are kept out. Section 84(2) deems certain matters to be disputes: a claim by the society for a debt or demand due from a member or his nominee/heirs; a claim by a surety against a principal debtor; and any dispute arising in connection with the election of an officer. Self-Help Group (SHG) / PACS savings-linked lending: An SHG is a small voluntary group (usually 10-20 women) that saves together and lends from the pooled savings, often with a bank loan (SHG-Bank Linkage supported by NABARD). Borrowing costs are modest — in practice SHG internal lending is commonly reported in a range around 12-24% per annum, with terms decided democratically by the group and many groups lowering rates over time. Benefits: small size, group guarantee instead of collateral, doorstep service, and financial discipline through mandatory savings. The group's own rules decide the rate, so it can be far cheaper than outside lenders. Cooperative bank / PACS (cooperative credit): Cooperative credit societies lend to their own members at rates decided within the society and consistent with RBI/cooperative-sector regulations. For crop loans, schemes like the Kisan Credit Card can bring the effective borrowing cost much lower through interest subvention (typically the farmer pays around 7% effective interest, with prompt repayment attracting an additional incentive), making it one of the cheapest and safest formal routes. Cooperative loans generally require membership, share capital, and proper documentation, and they keep a written record of every transaction. Local moneylender (sahukar/mahajan): Unlicensed, unregulated lenders. Their rates are not bound by any ceiling and are commonly reported in rural surveys to be several times the formal-bank rate — often around 24-60% or higher per annum in cash terms, sometimes expressed as a per-hundred-per-month charge that compounds. The money can be quick and requires no paperwork, but the moneylender commonly takes high collateral in the form of land papers, crops at low prices, or jewellery, and some add interest to unpaid interest (compounding), collect through pressure, and keep no written record —

Credit Score and CIBIL A credit score is a three-digit number (in India typically on a scale of 300 to 900) that summarises how reliably a person has repaid past loans. The best-known provider is TransUnion CIBIL, but scores are also generated by Experian, Equifax, and CRIF High Mark — in common speech all scores are often called the "CIBIL score". Banks and cooperatives use the score and the credit report (CIBIL report) to decide whether to lend and at what rate. A higher score (roughly above 750 is considered good) usually means easier loans, faster approval, lower interest, and better terms. What builds a score: timely repayment history (paying EMIs and loan instalments on or before due dates), the mix of credit used (a combination of a crop loan or Kisan Credit Card, a small vehicle or gold loan, and perhaps a debit-linked credit facility is fine), keeping outstanding balances low relative to the limit, a longer credit history, and not making too many loan applications in a short period, because each application creates a hard enquiry that can slightly lower the score. A person with no loan history at all has no score — so a farmer who has never borrowed formally may be rejected simply because the bank cannot judge him, not because he is unreliable. How a rural user can build and protect the score: - Take a small formal loan (KCC, MUDRA Shishu, gold loan, or a first vehicle loan) and repay every instalment on time. - Never miss the interest payment on a crop loan; even one delay gets recorded and repeated delays push the score down. - If a payment is late, pay as soon as possible rather than ignoring it — longer overdue periods damage the

Year 2: 53,500 × 1.07 = ₹57,245 (interest ₹3,745). Year 3: ≈ ₹61,252. Year 4: ≈ ₹65,540. Year 5: ≈ ₹70,128. Total compound interest over 5 years ≈ ₹20,128, whereas simple interest on the same ₹50,000 at 7% for 5 years is only (50,000 × 7 × 5) / 100 = ₹17,500. The compounding effect alone adds about ₹2,628 more. The gap grows wider with larger amounts, higher rates, or longer periods because each year's interest itself starts earning interest. The power of compounding cuts both ways: - For savers and investors, it is a friend. A deposit held for 10-15 years grows far more than simple addition suggests, so starting to save small amounts early is the single best habit a young farmer can build. - For borrowers, it is an enemy. A loan where unpaid interest is added to the principal can balloon quickly, which is exactly how some rural borrowers get trapped when a small debt becomes unmanageable. Always pay at least the interest due each month and prefer loans that clearly state how often interest accrues (daily, monthly, or annually). Key insight: the rule of 72. Divide 72 by the yearly rate to approximate how many years it takes a sum to double. At 6%, money doubles in about 12 years; at 12%, in about 6 years. This makes it easy to compare the true cost or return of any rate without a calculator. Monthly compounding (as used in many bank deposits) works on the same formula with n = 12: A = P × (1 + r/n)^(n×t). ## 3. Funding and channel: traditionally, long-term investment credit was the business of the long-term cooperative structure (PCARDBs/SCARDBs). In practice PACS also give medium/long-term finance or forward the member's requirement to the DCCB and the financing bank, because the funds a PACS lend come from the DCCB/SCB chain and are refinanced by NABARD. The KCC has also been widened to cover term loans for farm machinery and equipment, so a member may get durable credit through the same card. The exact product (society loan, DCCB loan or refinanced term loan) varies by state. Documentation: because these are bigger, longer loans, the society needs more evidence than for a crop loan. A member applying for a term loan is normally asked for: - A written application stating purpose and amount; the society's loan application form. - Proof of identity and membership (Aadhaar, photograph, membership/share certificate). - Title/possession evidence for land — land records, patadar passbook/patta, khasra details. - For land development or irrigation — a cost estimate, sometimes a technical report for wells/borings. - For machinery — quotations or invoices for the tractor/pump/implement to be purchased. - Repayment plan and, where required, guarantors. Security mirrors the purpose: a mortgage of land/property for big loans and hypothecation of the purchased asset (for example the machinery or pump) for others, with guarantors when the board requires them. The provision is invoked by the State through a formal notification (typically where more than 75% of the crop-sown area of the notified unit remains unsown), and payment to affected insured farmers is made within 30 days of the notification. Once the prevented-sowing claim is paid, the insurance cover for that crop terminates for the season. - **Mid-season adversity (on-account payment).** If adverse seasonal conditions — floods, prolonged dry spells, severe drought, etc. — occur mid-season and the expected yield of the affected crop is likely to fall below **50% of the normal/threshold yield**, the State may issue a damage notification and an "on-account" payment (up to 25% of the likely final claim) is released within about one month, later adjusted against the end-of-season yield-based claim. This provision is not invoked within 15 days of the normal harvest time. - **Localized calamities.** Loss to notified crops from localized risks of **hailstorm, landslide, inundation, cloudburst and natural fire due to lightning** affecting isolated farms in the notified area. These are assessed on an individual-farm basis through a joint survey, and liability is limited to the proportionate Sum Insured linked to the cost of inputs incurred up to the occurrence of the peril. Long-term loans Long-term (investment) loans at a PACS are given for durable assets and land improvement whose benefit lasts several years. The idea is that the asset itself increases the farm's productivity, and the increased income repays the loan in instalments. Common purposes: - Land development — land levelling, bunding, drainage, soil conservation and reclamation of waste land. - Irrigation — digging of wells and borewells, installation of pumps and motors, and micro-irrigation such as drip and sprinkler systems. - Farm machinery — tractors, power tillers, threshers, seed drills and other implements. - Post-harvest assets — farm godowns, silos, drying yards. - Allied and rural activities — orchards and plantation, livestock purchase and sheds, fisheries and poultry, depending on the by-laws. Tenure: the term matches the expected life of the asset and the stream of income it produces. Medium-term loans are commonly 3–5 years; long-term loans can run up to 10–15 years. The period varies with the purpose, the member's repayment capacity and state/refinance norms, so no single tenure applies. Repayment is by instalments — monthly, half-yearly or harvest-linked — and the principal is reduced over the loan period, with interest on the reducing balance. Funding and channel: traditionally, long-term investment credit was the business of the long-term cooperative structure (PCARDBs/SCARDBs). In practice PACS also give medium/long-term finance or forward the member's requirement to the DCCB

The Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 — Overview, Objects and Applicability The Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 (Act 39 of 2002) is the Central law governing co-operative societies whose objects are not confined to one State. It received Presidential assent on 3 July 2002, extends to the whole of India, and was brought into force from 19 August 2002. It repealed and replaced the Multi-unit Co-operative Societies Act, 1942 and the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 1984 (sections 103 and 126). A "multi-State co-operative society" is a society registered or deemed to be registered under this Act (section 3(p)), and includes a "national co-operative society" (a society specified in the Second Schedule, e.g., IFFCO, NAFED, KRIBHCO, NCUI) and a "federal co-operative" whose membership is open only to societies (sections 23–24). A "co-operative society" simpliciter means a society registered under a State law (section 3(h)); a "co-operative bank" is a multi-State society doing banking business (section 3(f)). Financial Structure — Funds, Reserves and Distribution of Net Profits (ss. 62–67) Non-profit discipline. The Act preserves the co-operative rule that a society is not a dividend-maximising company: no part of the funds, other than net profits, may be divided among members by way of bonus, dividend or otherwise (section 62(1)). "Net profits" are gross profits less overdue-interest accruals, establishment charges, interest on loans and deposits, audit fees, working expenses (repairs, rent, taxes, depreciation), employee bonus and the bonus equalisation fund, income-tax provision and approved donations, development rebate, and provisions for the development, bad debt, price-fluctuation, dividend-equalisation, share-capital redemption, investment-fluctuation and retirement-benefit funds, after writing off bad debts and losses not adjusted against a fund created out of profits (section 62(2)). A retiring auditor must be re-appointed unless disqualified, unwilling, replaced by resolution, or the proposed replacement cannot act (sections 70–71). Qualifications. The auditor must be a chartered accountant (section 72). A body corporate, an officer or employee of the society, a person employed by such officer/employee, a person indebted to the society, or a person guaranteeing a third person's debt to the society beyond one thousand rupees, is disqualified; disqualification after appointment vacates office. Powers and duties. The auditor has a right of access at all times to the books, accounts and vouchers wherever kept, and may require any information and explanations from officers and employees (section 73). The auditor must inquire whether loans and advances are properly secured and on terms not prejudicial to the society or members, whether transactions represented by book entries alone are prejudicial, whether personal expenses have been charged to revenue, and whether shares said to be allotted for cash have actually received the cash. The auditor reports to the members on the balance-sheet and profit and loss account, and the report must state whether the accounts present a true and fair view and whether proper books have been kept, branch returns are adequate, and the balance-sheet agrees with the books; reasons must be given for qualified or negative answers. Only the appointed auditor may sign the audit report (section 74). The report is read before the general meeting and is open to inspection by members (section 75); the auditor is entitled to receive meeting notices, attend general meetings and be heard (section 76). Remuneration is fixed by the board or Central Registrar where they appoint, otherwise by the general meeting. Regularity and downstream consequences. The money can be quick and requires no paperwork, but the moneylender commonly takes high collateral in the form of land papers, crops at low prices, or jewellery, and some add interest to unpaid interest (compounding), collect through pressure, and keep no written record — practices that fuel rural debt traps. In the worst cases, non-payment leads to loss of land or repeated dependency. Why formal credit matters: - Written agreements, fixed interest, no hidden redefinition of the debt, and legal remedies if a lender misbehaves. - Formal loans (bank, cooperative, RRB, PACS) are supervised; their interest rates are far more predictable. - A paid loan builds your credit history (see the credit score topic), which makes the next loan cheaper. - Government support (interest subvention, guarantee, insurance) reaches only through formal channels. - Moneylenders fill a gap that the cooperative movement exists to close: cooperative members should first approach their PACS, cooperative bank, or SHG before any outside lender. ## 8. Nearly all rural households are eligible, and cooperatives, RRBs, and post offices participate in delivery.
